lessons.title: Why plants need acclimatising
lessons.html:
From the nursery to the office

Interior plantscaping means placing living plants inside offices, malls, hotels and homes. Most of these plants are grown in shade houses or tunnels where there is a lot of light, warmth, humidity and fertiliser. Inside a building there is much less light, the air is dry from air conditioning, and there is less water and feeding.

If a plant moves straight from the tunnel to an office, it gets a shock. It drops leaves, turns yellow and may die. Acclimatising means slowly getting the plant used to the new conditions before it goes inside.

What changes for the plant

FactorNurseryBuilding
LightHighLow
HumidityHighLow (dry air)
WaterOftenLess often
FertiliserLots, for fast growthLittle, for slow growth
TemperatureChanges day and nightSteady

Signs of shock

  • Leaves turning yellow and falling
  • Brown leaf tips and edges
  • Long, thin, weak new growth stretching to the light
  • Wilting even when the soil is wet

Plants that are commonly used indoors in South Africa include ficus, dracaena, spathiphyllum (peace lily), zamioculcas (ZZ plant), sansevieria, philodendron and palms such as kentia. Each one handles low light differently, so ask your supervisor which plants can go where.

lessons.title: The acclimatising process
lessons.html:
Step by step

  1. Choose healthy plants. Check for pests, disease, damaged leaves and good roots. Never acclimatise a sick plant.
  2. Move to more shade. Put the plants under heavier shade cloth (for example from 40% to 70–80% shade) or into an acclimatising house. Do this for the time your supervisor sets, usually several weeks for big plants.
  3. Cut back fertiliser. Give less feeding so growth slows down and the plant does not make soft, weak leaves.
  4. Water less often. Let the top of the potting mix dry a little between waterings. Indoor plants are more often killed by too much water than too little.
  5. Lower the humidity slowly. Reduce misting and keep plants away from wet floors.
  6. Clean and check. Remove dead leaves. Look under leaves for mealybug, scale and red spider mite.
  7. Record. Write the date the plant started and any problems on the batch card.

Moving the plant

  • Wrap or sleeve the plant so leaves do not break.
  • Keep it out of wind, hot sun and cold during transport. Do not leave plants in a closed bakkie in the sun.
  • Place it in the building where the light suits that plant. Keep it away from air-conditioning vents and heaters.

Safety

  • Lift big pots with two people or a trolley.
  • Some plants have sap that irritates the skin (for example dieffenbachia and euphorbia). Wear gloves and wash your hands.

Key points

  • Acclimatising slowly prepares nursery plants for low light and dry air indoors.
  • Increase shade step by step and reduce fertiliser and water.
  • Only acclimatise healthy, pest-free plants.
  • Protect plants during transport and keep them away from air-con vents.
